node.label: Robert H Wiebe
node.date_label: Businessmen and Reform (1962) · The Search for Order (1967) · Self-Rule (1995)
node.description: Historian of American social organization and democracy. Northwestern’s archival biography identifies The Search for Order as an interpretation of the transition from local communities toward bureaucratic organization. Ashley Woodiwiss’s substantial reading of Self-Rule emphasizes tensions between participatory self-government, centralization and hierarchy, while retaining the racial and gender exclusions of earlier democracy. These are historically argued models, not inevitable stages.

incident_edges.relationship: Self-Rule interprets American democracy through participatory institutions and the constraints of centralization and hierarchy.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Ashley Woodiwiss1996 reading; earlier white-male democracy’s exclusions remain explicit rather than an idealized universal democracy.

incident_edges.relationship: Wiebe connects changing work relations and social hierarchies to the possibilities of democratic self-government.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Woodiwiss’s Self-Rule discussion of transformed work, voluntary groups and the modern class system; substantive social interpretation, not merely a department label.

incident_edges.relationship: Rodgers builds on Wiebe’s account of organizational change while treating bureaucratic social efficiency as one progressive language among several.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own1982 historiographical essay,117–118 and127/n59, praises the link between organizational transformation and one strand of thought while explicitly noting that Wiebe had already made qualifications that later inquiries swamped. This specified resource coexists with Rodgers’s criticism of simplification; it does not make Wiebe responsible for Rodgers’s entire three-language interpretation. The Search for Order and later1973 essay remain unread here.

incident_edges.relationship: Rodgers argues that Wiebe’s organizational synthesis simplified progressive ideas and left the relation between professionalization and social visions insufficiently explained.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own1982 essay,118–119, qualifies the new-middle-class carrier thesis and distinguishes job control from a shared bureaucratic political ethos. He praises Wiebe’s account of organizational change and later credits his earlier qualifications,n59; this is not a wholesale rejection. Hays’s more sweeping functionalist explanation is a separate target and is not silently assigned to Wiebe.
